lesson.title: Ninety Degrees, One Decade at a Time: The Bode Phase Plot
lesson.summary: A Bode phase plot graphs phase angle against a logarithmic frequency axis, using a three segment straight line approximation that is exact at the corner frequency and off by less than six degrees everywhere else.
lesson.body:
Phase Response gave the exact phase angle of the RC low pass filter at several frequencies, and Decade again supplies the natural logarithmic unit for the horizontal axis. A Bode Phase Plot graphs theta(w) = -arctan(wRC) against a log frequency axis, and just like the magnitude plot, it has a standard straight line approximation used for hand sketching, though this one uses three segments instead of two: flat at 0 degrees for frequencies at or below one tenth of the corner frequency, a straight sloped line from one tenth of the corner up to ten times the corner, and flat again at -90 degrees for frequencies at or above ten times the corner. This three segment shape mirrors the two segment magnitude asymptote closely enough that the two plots are almost always presented together, stacked one above the other on the same frequency axis.

For the running example, R = 1000 ohms, C = 1 microfarad, corner frequency wc = 1000 rad/s, the sloped middle segment of the asymptote runs from w = 100 rad/s, one tenth of wc, up to w = 10000 rad/s, ten times wc, a span of exactly two decades. Since the phase must move from 0 degrees to -90 degrees across those two decades, the asymptote's slope works out to -45 degrees per decade, and because the corner frequency sits exactly halfway between those two boundaries on a log scale, the straight line predicts theta = -45 degrees exactly at wc.

Check that midpoint prediction against the true value computed earlier: at w = 1000 rad/s, theta = -arctan(1) = -45.000 degrees. The straight line asymptote and the true curve agree exactly at the corner frequency, with zero error, which is the most useful landmark on the entire plot.

Now check the two boundary points, where the asymptote is known to be least accurate. At w = 100 rad/s, the asymptote predicts 0 degrees, since this is the flat lower segment's edge, but the true value computed in Phase Response is theta = -arctan(0.1) = -5.711 degrees, an error of 5.711 degrees. At w = 10000 rad/s, the asymptote predicts -90 degrees, the flat upper segment's edge, but the true value is theta = -arctan(10) = -84.289 degrees, an error of 5.711 degrees in the opposite direction. Both boundary errors have the identical magnitude, 5.711 degrees, which is not a coincidence, it follows from the symmetry of the arctangent function around wRC = 1.

That maximum error of about 5.7 degrees, occurring right at the two breakpoints of the three segment approximation, is a standard fact every circuit designer learns to expect. It means the straight line Bode phase plot is trustworthy everywhere, exact at the corner and within six degrees at its two worst points one decade to either side, which is more than adequate for the kind of quick, calculator free analysis these plots were designed to support. Between the breakpoints and the corner the true curve and the asymptote stay even closer together than the worst case value, so the 5.7 degree figure can be treated as a dependable upper bound on error across the entire sloped segment.
